title: Trump admin loses fight to spy on random journalists’ LinkedIn DMs
gist: A unanimous three-judge appeals panel led by Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III ordered the district court to substantially narrow a DOJ demand for 18 months of LinkedIn communications from journalists in a military-leak probe and to likely adopt LinkedIn's narrow alternative to a year-long secrecy order. Microsoft and press advocates hailed it as a landmark limit on dragnet demands to tech platforms.

insights.claim: The DOJ asked LinkedIn for 18 months of communications from targeted journalists who collectively published over 1,000 articles, extending to users with any possible link to those journalists around the time a leaked military report was drafted.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Shows the breadth of government data demands that tech platforms face.
insights.locator: The order came after the DOJ

insights.claim: The Trump administration obtained a secrecy order barring LinkedIn from disclosing the request for a year, leaving affected journalists unaware their First Amendment rights were compromised.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Gag orders raise legal and trust risk for platforms hosting sensitive communications.
insights.locator: The majority of journalists have LinkedIn accounts

themes.theme: Appeals court ruling and legal standard

insights.claim: A unanimous three-judge appeals panel led by Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III rejected quashing the order entirely but ordered the district court to substantially narrow the LinkedIn disclosure order to protect press freedoms.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Sets a precedent limiting broad government data requests to platforms.
insights.locator: Judge: Security and free speech can coexist

insights.claim: The appeals court held that district courts may not approve government records requests merely because they are logistically feasible for the company to compile.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Raises the bar for compelled data production, reducing compliance burdens for tech firms.
insights.quote: “It is not appropriate for district courts to approve requests purely because the records requested are logistically feasible to compile,”

insights.claim: Wilkinson wrote that wholesale collection of reporters' records to identify sources would harm democratic health, and that many targeted users had no conceivable relationship to the leak investigation.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Strengthens legal protection for confidential communications on platforms.
insights.quote: “A request by the government to scoop up reporters’ records wholesale and ascertain the identity of their sources would tip the balance against informed discourse in a manner inimical to democratic health.”

insights.claim: Unless the government gives a more persuasive justification on remand, LinkedIn's proposal to notify a single attorney of the investigated news outlet must be adopted as a narrow exception to the secrecy order.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Likely to weaken blanket gag orders on platforms in leak probes.
insights.locator: “Unless the government’s response to LinkedIn’s proposal

insights.claim: LinkedIn argued that most journalists publish contact details there to attract sources, so overbroad demands threaten a critical platform for confidential sourcing, an argument the judges accepted.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: User trust is core platform value; legal defense of it protects engagement.
insights.locator: The majority of journalists have LinkedIn accounts

insights.claim: Microsoft, LinkedIn's owner, called the ruling important for privacy and press freedom and does not appear to expect the government to defend the sweeping request on remand.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Microsoft positions itself as a privacy defender against government overreach.
insights.locator: LinkedIn, which is owned by Microsoft

insights.claim: RCFP President Bruce D. Brown predicted the ruling will quickly become a leading opinion on protecting confidential sources from dragnet demands to technology companies.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
entities: Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press
insights.so_what: Precedent could be cited broadly in future data requests to tech platforms.
insights.quote: “This ruling is a big deal and will quickly become one of the leading opinions in the area—one we will be quoting from it for a long time,”
insights.locator: Several civil rights groups backed LinkedIn

top_entities: Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press
